tldr: UniReflex is a universal plug-and-play framework that equips frozen generative robot policies with precise force control (variable impedance control) without any slow-backbone fine-tuning, driven by a fast reflex network running on non-invasively intercepted latent features.
hero_caption: System overview of UniReflex. Deep latent representations are intercepted right before the action head of a slow visual planning policy (e.g., DP, π0, DreamZero) and fed into a lightweight reflex network (GRU) running at ~50 Hz to predict target force and stiffness. An impedance control layer running at ~200 Hz tracks these outputs, enabling compliant, contact-adaptive behavior.
overview:
Generative models like Diffusion Policy and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel at planning smooth trajectories from camera images. However, when it comes to contact-rich tasks that require sustaining forces—such as peeling a sticky note or wiping a surface—they often fail. Conventional approaches simply track geometric position trajectories with fixed gains, causing the end-effector to lose contact or press too hard whenever small environmental misalignments or friction changes occur.

Retraining these massive models end-to-end with force sensor inputs is computationally expensive and risks degrading their general-purpose motor planning capabilities. The authors had a clever idea: why not non-invasively "peek" at the deep latent representations generated right before the action head of the smart brain (the generative model), and pass them to an independent, lightweight reflex circuit (a GRU)?

This is the core concept of UniReflex. Keeping the generative model's backbone completely frozen, UniReflex trains only a fast reflex layer using the intercepted latent features and wrist force sensor readings. This reflex layer predicts normalized anisotropic stiffness directions and target interaction forces in real time, tracking them via variable impedance control (VIC).

Evaluated on five contact-rich bimanual tasks, UniReflex improved success rates in the contact phase by 20% to 60% without sacrificing the original model's precise positioning capabilities. Furthermore, compared to joint fine-tuning strategies across the entire model, UniReflex achieves 25–66x lower per-step backward latency.
contributions: Established a plug-and-play framework that equips frozen generative policies with closed-loop force control simply by hooking latent representations from the action head.
Proposed a learning strategy to decouple active force exertion intent from anisotropic stiffness using teleoperation demonstration data, directly feeding into variable impedance control (VIC).
Introduced a contact-triggered adaptive gating mechanism that enables seamless transitions between position-dominant approach and force-dominant contact phases.

Demonstrated on real bimanual robots across three diverse generative backbones (DP, π0, and DreamZero) that UniReflex significantly boosts contact task success rates while preserving position accuracy and drastically slashing training costs.

sections.heading: Why Do Smart Robots Struggle with Contact Tasks?
sections.summary: While modern imitation learning policies excel at trajectory planning, they often break down in contact-rich tasks due to a lack of closed-loop force feedback. Existing force-aware methods require retraining the whole model, which degrades the strengths of large pretrained backbones. UniReflex addresses this by non-invasively extracting features from a frozen backbone to train only a lightweight reflex layer.
sections.details:
Generative imitation learning approaches, such as Diffusion Policy (DP) and VLAs, have achieved impressive success in tabletop pick-and-place tasks. However, their reliability plummets on contact-rich tasks like wiping, insertion, and peeling. The root cause is that the networks predict purely geometric position trajectories, which the low-level controller rigidly tracks with fixed gains. The slightest change in surface geometry or stiffness leads to unstable contact.

Prior attempts to address this include adding force sensor readings as inputs, using hybrid position/force control, and employing hierarchical fast-slow frameworks. Yet, these methods require redesigning the architecture or retraining end-to-end. Throwing away pretrained weights or heavily fine-tuning large foundation models is inefficient and damages general-purpose visual reasoning.

This motivated the authors to ask: can we add plug-and-play closed-loop force control to task-adapted slow generative models without modifying them at all? UniReflex non-invasively intercepts deep latent representations from the action generation head and uses this high-level intent to drive a lightweight reflex network. As a result, the robot acquires robust physical reflexes while preserving the original pretrained distribution intact.

sections.heading: How Does UniReflex Differ from Existing Force-Aware Approaches?
sections.summary: Existing force-aware methods generally fall into three categories: treating force as an extra input modality, using hybrid or variable impedance control, or building hierarchical fast-slow policies. All of them share the limitation of requiring joint co-training across the entire model. UniReflex fundamentally differs by keeping the slow backbone completely frozen and only training an add-on fast reflex layer.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main streams:

- **Generative Imitation Learning**: Models like Diffusion Policy, CVAEs, VLAs (e.g., π0), and video-predictive World Action Models (e.g., DreamZero) perform well, but their outputs remain kinematic trajectories, lacking closed-loop force regulation mechanisms.
- **Force-Aware Robot Control**: Classical impedance control, modern hybrid position/force control, and imitation learning with force modalities have been explored. However, they demand end-to-end co-training of perception and action, making them unsuitable as post-hoc modular add-ons for pretrained policies.
- **Hierarchical Fast-Slow Policies**: These decouple slow visual inference latency from millisecond-level contact feedback using asynchronous buffers or separate decoders. However, previous frameworks co-train both the slow and fast modules. This incurs massive computational costs on large backbones and makes deployment on existing models challenging.

UniReflex's key novelty lies in its "fast-only" training paradigm: the slow generative policy is completely frozen, and a compact reflex layer is trained using only intercepted latent features and wrist force feedback.

sections.heading: Shared Structure in Generative Action Heads and VIC Basics
sections.summary: Although diffusion and flow-based generative models differ in their training objectives, they converge to a temporally structured latent representation right before final action projection. In addition, this section reviews the fundamentals of variable impedance control (VIC), which treats the end-effector as a virtual spring-damper system to stabilize contact.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Commonality in Generative Action Heads
DP predicts noise ($\epsilon$), whereas π0 and DreamZero predict velocity vectors ($v_t$). Despite different loss functions, they both iteratively reconstruct action sequences from noise.

As the generation nears its final step ($k \to 0$), the internal states converge toward a clean action sequence, and the network's hidden layers store a deep, trajectory-level understanding. Right before the final fully connected layer projects this state to low-dimensional joint or end-effector coordinates, the network maintains a temporally structured latent representation $z \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T_{\mathrm{slow}} \times H}$. UniReflex taps into this representation non-invasively as the "slow intent."

### 3.2 Variable Impedance Control (VIC)
For contact-rich tasks, instead of operating the robot as a rigid position follower, it is effective to use variable impedance control to make it behave as a virtual spring-damper system. Let end-effector tracking error be $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ and external interaction force measured by a wrist sensor be $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}$. The system behaves compliantly according to a target stiffness matrix $K(t)$ alongside apparent inertia and damping parameters. UniReflex dynamically predicts both $K(t)$ and the target reference force $F_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

sections.heading: Feature Interception and the Reflex Network Architecture
sections.summary: Active pressing intent and stiffness labels are reconstructed from master-slave tracking errors in teleoperation data. Latent features intercepted from the frozen backbone are fed into a causal GRU to output high-frequency trajectory corrections, reference forces, and anisotropic stiffness. A contact-triggered gating mechanism stabilizes behavior across approach and execution.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Active Pressing Recovery and Anisotropic Stiffness Labels
To extract "where and how hard the robot intended to press" from demonstration logs, the authors examine the tracking displacement between the master device and slave arm ($\Delta x$). When running stiff tracking, this displacement directly reflects the virtual force (intent) exerted against the contact surface.

Stabilizing contact requires stiffening along the pressing axis while remaining compliant along orthogonal axes, rather than making the entire body soft. The authors build a diagonal stiffness template $\Phi_K$ that allocates high stiffness along the principal displacement axis $n = \Delta x / \|\Delta x\|$ and low stiffness along orthogonal directions, serving as the training target.

### 4.2 Non-Invasive Internal Representation Interception
Decomposing the noise predictor into $\Phi_{\mathrm{dec}}$ (deep multimodal reasoning) and $W_{\mathrm{out}}$ (projection to action space), UniReflex registers a PyTorch forward hook on the output of $\Phi_{\mathrm{dec}}$ at the final denoising step ($k \to 0$) to read the latent feature $z$. Because backbone weights remain unchanged, no architectural modifications to the original model are needed.

### 4.3 Intent-Conditioned Reflex Decoding
Generative models predict multi-step trajectory chunks open-loop, which cannot react to unexpected contact impacts. UniReflex's reflex layer (a causal GRU) takes three inputs at each high-frequency step:
- Time-aligned slow intent feature $s_t$
- Real-time wrist force and joint feedback $r_t$
- A learnable intra-chunk positional embedding $p_t$

The GRU processes these inputs to simultaneously predict an end-effector position offset $x_{\mathrm{reflex}}$, a reference interaction force $F_{\mathrm{ref}}$, and the stiffness parameter $\Phi_K$.

### 4.4 Contact-Triggered Adaptive Gating
The execution is divided into two phases. In "Phase I" (pre-contact approach), the system strictly follows the frozen generative policy's high-precision position trajectory. Once the wrist sensor detects contact, it switches to "Phase II." In Phase II, variable impedance control predominantly tracks $F_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and $\Phi_K$, while $x_{\mathrm{reflex}}$ applies fine trajectory adjustments in a hybrid control fashion.

Each task is evaluated using a two-stage protocol: pre-contact approach (position-dominant Phase I) and contact execution (force-dominant Phase II).

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Major Gains in Success and Force Tracking
sections.summary: Across five contact-rich tasks on a real bimanual robot, UniReflex improved contact-phase success rates by 20% to 60% and rapidly recovered contact forces under external disturbances. Furthermore, it reduced per-step backward latency by 25–66x compared to full-model fine-tuning.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on a real bimanual robot by attaching UniReflex to three representative backbones: Diffusion Policy (DP), π0, and DreamZero. End-to-end force-aware baselines (RDP, ForceVLA, and TA-VLA) were also evaluated. The benchmark comprised five tasks: Box Flipping, Charger Insertion, Sticky-note Peeling, Slanted Board Wiping, and Curved Board Wiping (200 demonstration episodes each).

### 5.2 Results and Analysis
- **Q1: Phase-Wise Task Performance**: In pre-contact Phase I, introducing UniReflex caused at most a 10 percentage point decrease, demonstrating that the base policy's approach accuracy remained well-preserved. In contact Phase II, success rates surged by 20% to 60% across all three backbones. The only task without dramatic improvement was Charger Insertion, which is dominated by brief impact transients and tight tolerances; the other four tasks involving sustained pressing saw substantial benefits.
- **Q2: Comparison with Monolithic Baselines**: Jointly retraining backbones with force inputs (ForceVLA, TA-VLA) severely degraded Phase I positioning accuracy. In contrast, UniReflex+DP and UniReflex+π0 outperformed or matched these baselines across both Phase I and Phase II.
- **Q3: Ablation Study**: Fixing stiffness to constant values or predicting only reference force (without stiffness) caused force tracking error rates to spike from 5.8–8.9% up to 28.3–38.7%, dropping Phase II success rates from 70–90% down to 20–50%. Removing the phase-switching gate and relying on the GRU from step zero crippled Phase I success rates (0–30%), underscoring the necessity of adaptive gating.
- **Q4 & Q5: Disturbance Robustness & Force Tracking**: When dynamic disturbances were applied by pushing boards or tilting tables mid-execution, the frozen DP lost contact and achieved only 10–20% success. UniReflex re-established target contact forces within 0.87–1.28 s, achieving an 80–100% recovery success rate.
- **Q6: Training Efficiency**: Measured on a single A800 GPU, UniReflex reduced backward latency per step by 25–66x compared to full joint fine-tuning. The trainable parameters accounted for only 0.188–0.375% of the total model, providing massive memory savings.

captions.F3: Fast reflex response and force tracking performance under external disturbances. (a) UniReflex maintains contact and recovers even when boards are tilted or pushed. (b) In the Sticky-note Peeling task, UniReflex closely tracks demonstration force trajectories compared to baselines. (c) Measured 3-axis forces align accurately with reference forces.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Horizons for UniReflex
sections.summary: When paired with models that have very long action chunking horizons like DreamZero, reflex responsiveness is constrained. The method also struggles with tasks dominated by high-impact transients like pin insertion, and overall performance remains bounded by hardware sensor noise and control loop bandwidth.
sections.details:
The authors identify three main limitations of UniReflex:

- **Latency in Long-Horizon World-Action Models**: In models like DreamZero with long visual inference intervals, backbone intent updates are slow. Consequently, the gains when tracking rapid environmental contact variations were smaller compared to DP or π0.
- **Unsuitability for Transient Impact Tasks**: Because UniReflex is tailored for sustained contact regulation, its efficacy is limited in tasks dominated by brief transient shocks and millimeter-level geometric tolerances, such as plug insertions.
- **Hardware Bandwidth Constraints**: The responsiveness of the reflex layer is fundamentally capped by physical factors, including wrist force sensor noise, communication latency, and the robot's low-level impedance control frequency (~200 Hz in this setup).

takeaways: Instead of retraining massive robot foundation models, intercepting latent features to drive an external fast reflex layer dramatically enhances contact skills without degrading high-level planning.
Decoupling active pressing intent and stiffness directions from teleoperation tracking errors ($\Delta x$) provides high-quality force supervision without specialized hardware.
Separating pre-contact position tracking from post-contact force regulation via an adaptive gate eliminates the trade-off between positioning precision and compliant contact.
Training only ~0.3% of the total parameters and slashing backward computation latency by tens of times makes UniReflex an exceptionally practical approach for upgrading deployed policies.
limitations: Offers limited improvement on stiff, transient-impact tasks with tight geometric tolerances, such as plug or pin insertion.
If the slow backbone's intent update interval is very long (e.g., large world-action models), the fast reflex layer cannot fully compensate for high-level divergence.
The system's dynamic tracking limit is bounded by wrist sensor sampling rates, communication latency, and low-level impedance control bandwidth.
